strengths: Introduces a principled, dataset-agnostic method for generating correlated-graph pairs (adapting Nowak et al.'s correlated Erdős-Rényi construction to arbitrary base graphs, including large graphs via BFS subgraph sampling), enabling graph alignment benchmarks across diverse real-world topologies rather than being restricted to synthetic random graphs.

The idea of tuning a controllable noise/difficulty parameter to find an 'optimal' regime that maximizes discriminative power between architectures is a nice, practically useful observation, and is empirically supported across multiple base datasets (Fig. 3, Table D.3).

Provides a clean theoretical justification (Theorem A.1) that the siamese training/evaluation pipeline respects the natural equivariance of the graph alignment problem, which is a rigorous and correct addition rather than just an empirical trick.

The application of the learned alignment embeddings as positional encodings (GAPE) is a creative reuse of a self-supervised structural task, and the ablations (Table E.5, Fig. E.1) exploring which pretraining dataset/noise-level to use are reasonably thorough and informative.

Extensive reproducibility material: detailed hyperparameters, compute resources, dataset generation parameters, and an accompanying open-source package are described, which aids verification and reuse by the community.

GAPE shows consistent improvements over standard positional encodings (Laplacian, RWPE, SignNet) on three molecular regression benchmarks even though it is restricted to 1-WL expressive power, which is a nontrivial and interesting empirical finding.
weaknesses: The headline PCQM4Mv2 'state-of-the-art' claim (Table 2) is extraordinary and under-justified: a 6.2M-parameter model using only 2D structure and no bonding/edge information reportedly nearly halves the MAE of much larger models (e.g., TGT-At at 203M params, 0.0671 MAE) that use richer features (3D information, bond types, advanced chemistry-informed encodings). Such a large, suspicious jump warrants official leaderboard submission/verification, clarification of exactly which split (validation vs. test-dev) is used for all compared numbers, and a much more careful analysis of why a simple 2D-only transformer would outperform models leveraging 3D/edge features so dramatically; as presented, this raises concerns about a fair/apples-to-apples comparison or potential subtle data leakage/setup discrepancy.

The comparison table (Table 2) mixes results from different papers using possibly different evaluation protocols (train/test splits, use of 3D geometry, ensembling) without clearly verifying they are directly comparable, which undermines the soundness of the significance claims in the abstract/introduction.

The benchmarking study in Section 5 is limited to five 1-WL-bounded MPNN architectures; conclusions about anisotropic vs isotropic models, while interesting, are drawn from a fairly narrow architecture pool and the paper does not test more expressive/attention-based graph transformers or higher-order GNNs, despite motivating the need for finer-grained comparisons among architectures in the same WL class.

The criterion for selecting the 'optimal noise level' is described qualitatively (largest accuracy gap, non-overlapping error bars) rather than through a formal, automatable metric, making the benchmarking protocol somewhat subjective and harder to standardize across new datasets/architectures.

Some claimed comparisons are incomplete: SPE and PEARL positional encodings could not be evaluated on PCQM4Mv2/ZINC due to OOM errors, weakening the completeness of the positional-encoding comparison in Table 1, and no runtime/compute-cost comparison is given between GAPE pretraining and computing simpler baselines (e.g., Laplacian eigenvectors), even though GAPE requires an additional pretraining stage.

The paper's argument that structural-only benchmarks 'generalize' to real downstream tasks with different features is plausible but not rigorously validated; the only direct evidence connecting alignment-task performance to downstream task performance is the GAPE positional-encoding experiments, which is a relatively indirect and narrow test of this broader generalization claim.

Presentation could be improved in places: notation is dense (e.g., overloading N, several similar symbols for adjacency/permutation matrices), and some claims made confidently in the main text (e.g., 'anisotropic GNNs enable a finer understanding of structural features') would benefit from additional statistical testing beyond visual inspection of confidence intervals across a larger set of architectures/seeds.

strengths: The core idea of using the Graph Alignment Problem as a topology-agnostic combinatorial pretext task for benchmarking GNN structural understanding is conceptually appealing and addresses a real gap (existing SBM/CSL-based structural benchmarks cannot easily match diverse real-world topologies).

The methodology for turning any base graph dataset into a family of graph-alignment datasets with controllable difficulty (edge add/remove noise model, BFS sub-sampling for large graphs) is reasonably general and is accompanied by an open-source package with fairly detailed hyperparameters, which aids reproducibility.
The equivariance proof (Theorem A.1), while elementary, is a useful sanity check that the proposed siamese training/evaluation procedure is consistent with the underlying combinatorial problem.

The empirical study spans several base topologies (synthetic ER, citation graphs, molecular graphs) and several canonical MPNN architectures, and the 'accuracy gap' analysis to identify an informative noise regime is a sensible practical heuristic.

The idea of repurposing the learned alignment embeddings as positional encodings (GAPE) for downstream graph transformers is a novel and interesting use of the benchmark task beyond pure ranking of architectures.
weaknesses: The headline PCQM4Mv2 result (MAE 0.0337 vs. best published baselines around 0.067–0.086, using far fewer parameters and no bond/edge features) is an implausibly large jump given that GAPE itself is explicitly acknowledged to be bounded by 1-WL expressivity while the compared positional encodings (SignNet, RWPE, etc.) are strictly more expressive. Such a large gap over heavily tuned, well-established SOTA systems demands much more rigorous validation (independent re-implementation checks, ablations isolating the transformer/backbone from the encoding, sanity checks against label leakage through the graph-alignment pretraining pipeline, matched training budgets) that the paper does not provide; as presented, this central claim is not adequately supported by the evidence.

Comparisons to prior SOTA methods in Table 2 are not apples-to-apples: baselines are taken from their original papers with their own training budgets/architectures, while the proposed model was trained with a different, non-disclosed-in-detail large-scale multi-GPU regime (3 GPUs, ~2 days), making the 'state-of-the-art with fewer parameters' claim difficult to trust as a controlled comparison.

The benchmarking methodology's real-world validity is only exercised in one downstream setting (positional encodings for molecular regression); no experiment verifies that alignment-task rankings actually predict performance on the social-network/citation-graph downstream tasks (e.g., node classification on CoraFull/OGBN-Arxiv) for which two of the five base datasets were specifically chosen, leaving the paper's central benchmarking claim under-validated for a large fraction of the datasets studied.

The noise model used to construct correlated graphs (choice of padd/premove, and the switch between 'stable degree' and 'no removal' regimes) is a heuristic design choice without theoretical justification for why it faithfully represents 'difficulty' or is comparable in meaning across very different topologies (ER vs. molecular vs. citation graphs), undermining the comparability of the difficulty axis across domains that is central to the paper's ranking methodology.

Architectural conclusions (anisotropic > isotropic GNNs) are drawn from five architectures that differ in more than just isotropy (attention heads, parameterization, gating), so the causal attribution of the performance gap to anisotropy specifically is not well isolated/controlled.

Some baseline PE methods (SPE, PEARL) are excluded from two of three datasets due to OOM errors rather than being adapted/optimized to fit within memory constraints, weakening the fairness of the Table 1 comparison; on ZINC, GAPE alone actually underperforms SignNet, a limitation that is understated in the surrounding narrative.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem A.1) is a fairly standard equivariance argument for permutation-equivariant models and does not add substantial technical depth beyond motivating the architectural design choice already used in prior work (Nowak et al. 2017).

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely novel benchmarking methodology centered on the Graph Alignment Problem, which cleverly decouples structural understanding from feature learning while remaining applicable to arbitrary real-world graph topologies (unlike SBM-based PATTERN/CLUSTER or CSL). The method for generating correlated graphs at controllable noise levels from any base dataset (including large-scale graphs via BFS sampling) is a solid, generalizable technical contribution.

Theoretical grounding is provided: Theorem A.1 rigorously establishes that the siamese training/evaluation procedure respects the equivariance of the underlying Graph Alignment Problem, which is an important sanity check often missing from purely empirical benchmark papers.

The empirical benchmarking study is extensive: 40 generated datasets (5 base graph types × 8 noise levels), 5 canonical MPNN architectures, 10 repeated runs each, with full results in the appendix. The identification of an 'optimal noise level' where model ranking is most statistically distinguishable and generalizes to other noise levels is a useful, non-trivial practical finding.

The downstream application (GAPE) is compelling and practically significant: the learned alignment embeddings outperform widely used positional encodings (LAP, RWPE, SignNet, etc.) on three molecular regression tasks, and a simple transformer using GAPE reportedly surpasses several much larger SOTA models on PCQM4Mv2 with an order of magnitude fewer parameters — a strong demonstration of the practical value of the benchmarking task beyond pure evaluation.
Reproducibility is well supported: detailed hyperparameters, compute resources, and an open-source Python package are provided, and the NeurIPS-style checklist is thoroughly completed.

Ablation studies (Table E.5, Figure E.1) sensibly show that GAPE performance depends on matching the pre-training graph topology and noise level to the downstream task, adding useful practical guidance rather than just a headline result.
weaknesses: The SOTA comparison in Table 2 is not entirely apples-to-apples: the proposed model uses only 2D graph structure while several baselines (e.g., Uni-Mol+, EGT, TGT) leverage additional chemistry-derived features or edge/bonding information. Although this is mentioned as a strength (avoiding domain-specific preprocessing), it complicates a fully fair head-to-head parameter/performance comparison.

The flagship PCQM4Mv2 result (Table 2) is based on only 2 runs per model size, which is a fairly small sample for a claim of state-of-the-art performance, especially compared to the more rigorous 10-run protocol used in the core benchmarking experiments (Section 5).

The notion of 'optimal noise level' driving model selection and ranking is somewhat post-hoc — it is determined by inspecting the accuracy-gap curves after training rather than derived from a principled criterion, which could limit its use as a truly hands-off benchmarking recipe for new topologies.

The core benchmarking experiments use relatively small models (~60K parameters, 4 layers) to rank architectures; it is unclear whether the anisotropic-vs-isotropic ranking conclusions generalize to larger, more heavily tuned architectures typically used in practice.

Comparisons to some very recent, more expressive positional encoding baselines (SPE, PEARL) could not be completed due to OOM errors on PCQM4Mv2/ZINC, leaving a gap in the completeness of the positional-encoding comparison for exactly the datasets where the strongest claims are made.

The broader claim that structural-only benchmarking results generalize to real downstream task performance (motivated by Figure 1) is intuitively argued but only indirectly validated through the GAPE experiments; a more direct correlation analysis between alignment-task ranking and downstream task ranking across more architectures would strengthen this central claim.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated benchmarking methodology: reframing graph alignment as a self-supervised, structure-only task that can be instantiated on arbitrary real-world topologies (not just Erdős-Rényi or SBM graphs as in prior combinatorial benchmarks), with a controllable difficulty knob (noise level η).

Solid theoretical grounding: equivariance proofs for the siamese architecture (Thm A.1), invariance to graph automorphisms (Thm B.2), and a clean link between the WL hierarchy and achievable alignment accuracy/loss (Thm C.1, Corollary C.2), giving principled justification for why the task probes structural expressivity.

Extensive empirical validation: 40 generated datasets across 5 base topologies and 8 noise levels, benchmarking of standard MPNNs plus additional architectures (GraphGPS, PNA, SGC, higher-order GSN/PPGN) in the appendix, and an explicit demonstration that model rankings at the 'optimal' noise level are stable across noise levels.

Goes beyond pure benchmarking to show practical utility: the learned embeddings (GAPE) are competitive with or better than strong existing positional encodings (LAP, SignNet, RWPE, GPSE) on molecular regression tasks, and achieve near-perfect (>94% F1) edge reconstruction, supporting the claim that the task captures meaningful structural information rather than being an arbitrary puzzle.

Reasonably honest limitations section and appendix material (e.g., theoretical bound on when the planted alignment is truly optimal, OOM failures of baselines disclosed rather than hidden) and promise of an open-source package for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The 'optimal noise level' η*, central to the benchmarking claims and to selecting the best GAPE model, is determined empirically post hoc with no closed-form or principled selection rule; the paper only argues it 'varies little' within a topological family and can be warm-started, which is a fairly weak reproducibility guarantee for practitioners applying the method to new datasets.

Downstream validation of GAPE is restricted almost entirely to molecular regression (AQSOL, ZINC, PCQM4Mv2), despite the paper generating alignment datasets from citation/social graphs (CoraFull, OGBN-Arxiv) for the benchmarking study; there is no downstream task evaluation on non-molecular domains, limiting evidence that the representational claims generalize broadly.

Several comparisons appear to involve many researcher degrees of freedom (per-dataset choice of GNN architecture, embedding dimension, and noise level for generating GAPE in Table K.10/L.13), which raises some risk of favorable cherry-picking rather than a fully controlled ablation.

The explanation for GPSE outperforming GAPE+RWPE on ZINC (that GPSE's pre-training objective includes cycle counting, an 'unfair advantage') is a plausible but post-hoc, somewhat self-serving rationalization not independently verified.

Correlation analysis between alignment accuracy and downstream MAE (Appendix I) is based on very few architecture/scale points per plot (order of 6-8), so the reported Pearson correlations, while strong, rest on limited statistical power.

The method is explicitly acknowledged to be impractical for graphs beyond ~10,000 nodes due to the O(N^2) similarity matrix, requiring BFS subsampling; this limits applicability to very large-scale graphs and could distort structural statistics for such graphs.

The paper's main text is dense and defers most of the substantive empirical/theoretical support to a very long appendix, which somewhat hampers self-contained readability and assessment from the main submission alone.

strengths: The core idea of using the graph alignment problem as a topology-controllable, feature-free benchmarking task for GNNs is well-motivated and clearly distinguished from existing combinatorial-optimization benchmarks (SBM-based PATTERN/CLUSTER, CSL, TSP, SAT), which are noted to be tied to a narrow set of topologies or lack tunable difficulty.

The noising procedure for generating correlated graph pairs from arbitrary base graph datasets (including a BFS-based sampling scheme for large graphs) is a genuinely useful and reasonably general contribution that extends beyond the Erdős-Rényi-only setting of prior work (Nowak et al., 2017).

The theoretical results (equivariance of the Siamese architecture, invariance of the loss under automorphisms, and a WL-hierarchy bound linking expressivity to achievable alignment accuracy) provide reasonable formal grounding for the proposed pipeline.

The empirical study spans multiple topological families (Erdős-Rényi, molecular graphs, citation networks) and a reasonably large set of architectures/scales, and the identification of an 'optimal noise level' for statistically distinguishing architectures is an interesting empirical observation with practical implications for benchmark design.

Downstream validation of the learned embeddings (GAPE) as positional encodings for graph transformers, plus near-perfect adjacency reconstruction from frozen embeddings, provides some evidence that the pretext task captures transferable structural information rather than being purely a self-referential puzzle.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim ('anisotropic architectures are intrinsically better at structural understanding than isotropic ones') rests on comparisons among a small, somewhat dated set of MPNNs (GCN, GIN, GatedGCN, GAT, GATv2) with fixed parameter budgets; confounds such as parameter allocation per layer, effective receptive field, and hyperparameter tuning per model are not fully controlled for, so the isotropic/anisotropic dichotomy as the causal explanation is not rigorously isolated.

The claimed generalization/robustness properties of the 'optimal noise level' (that rankings transfer across noise levels and that no full sweep is needed) are argued largely via visual inspection of a handful of plots and prose assertions rather than a quantitative correlation/statistical test (e.g., rank correlation across noise levels with confidence intervals), weakening the rigor of a key selling point of the benchmark.

The task is fundamentally structure-only (features are erased), which is explicitly framed as a design virtue, but this substantially limits the significance of the ranking results for practitioners who care about GNN performance on real, feature-rich tasks; the transfer to feature-based downstream performance is only indirectly and partially supported (Section I regression/correlation is presented only for a narrow set of models/datasets, largely in the appendix, and effectively functions as a secondary, under-scrutinized claim).

GAPE's advantage over strong baselines (SignNet, GPSE, RWPE) in Table 1 is modest in most cases (e.g., within noise of standard deviations) and the paper does not fully control for the pretraining compute/data budget differences among methods (GPSE, SPE, PEARL) when explaining the OOM issues and performance gaps, making the 'GAPE is competitive despite being 1-WL bounded' claim somewhat overstated.

Important supporting experiments (higher-order GNN comparisons, correlation with downstream tasks, choice of pretraining dataset) are relegated entirely to the appendix and are thinly described (e.g., Table H.9 and Section I show only single-run or minimally-repeated results without variance estimates in several cases), reducing confidence in their robustness and making the main paper's narrative rely on appendix material that is not fully vetted to the same standard as the main results.

The paper's writing repeatedly makes strong qualitative claims ('near-perfect reconstruction', 'this confirms...', 'a fundamental pre-training objective') that outpace the actual quantitative evidence provided (e.g., 94% F1 is good but not clearly 'near-perfect' for structure recovery, and single dataset-pair reconstruction experiments do not establish generality across topologies beyond ZINC/PCQM4Mv2).

The reproducibility of the large hyperparameter/dataset generation pipeline (40+ datasets, multiple architectures, multiple noise levels, multiple downstream tasks) depends heavily on the released code, which is not inspectable in this review; the paper text alone leaves some generation choices (e.g., how exactly padd/premove interact with disconnected components, or how the 'optimal noise level' is operationally selected before running the full sweep it claims to avoid) insufficiently specified for independent replication from the manuscript alone.

strengths: Well-motivated and genuinely novel benchmarking framework: the graph alignment task naturally generalizes the graph isomorphism problem and the WL test, and unlike prior combinatorial-optimization benchmarks (PATTERN/CLUSTER/CSL/SAT/TSP) it can be layered onto *any* existing graph dataset without altering topology, while also offering a tunable difficulty knob (noise level η). This directly closes a documented gap in the GNN benchmarking literature (Table C.2).

Strong theoretical grounding: the paper proves equivariance/invariance properties of the Siamese training scheme (Thm 3.1/3.2, A.1, B.2), formally connects task difficulty to the WL hierarchy (Thm C.1/Cor C.2), and gives a metric-learning interpretation, which lends principled support to the empirical design choices rather than treating them as ad hoc.

Extensive and largely consistent empirical validation: forty benchmark datasets across 5 base topologies and 8 noise levels, a clear finding that there exists an 'optimal noise level' maximizing statistical separability between architectures, and that this ranking is stable across noise levels — a genuinely useful practical guideline for benchmark design.

Good breadth of follow-up experiments in the appendix that substantiate the main claims: extended architecture sweep (PNA, GraphGPS, SGC) at two size budgets, higher-order GNN comparisons (PPGN, GSN) showing the benchmark differentiates within/across WL classes, and a correlation study (Appendix I) linking Graph Alignment accuracy to downstream MAE with strong Pearson correlations.

Demonstrated downstream utility beyond the benchmarking use case: GAPE positional encodings are competitive with or better than several established PE methods (LAP, RWPE, SignNet) on molecular regression, and near-perfect (>94% F1) graph reconstruction from frozen GAPE embeddings supports the claim that the task induces meaningful structural compression rather than 'puzzle-solving'.

Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, dataset generation procedures, and an accompanying open-source package are provided, along with fairly thorough appendices documenting experimental settings.
weaknesses: The 'optimal noise level' concept, while empirically useful, lacks a principled a priori determination method; the paper acknowledges 'η* admits no closed form' and relies on warm-starting/sweeping, which somewhat undercuts the claim of a rigorous, prescriptive benchmarking protocol for new topologies.

The comparison in Table 1 is not uniformly favorable to GAPE — GPSE outperforms GAPE+RWPE on ZINC, and the explanation (GPSE's cycle-counting pretext task overlapping with the ZINC target) is plausible but not independently verified; additionally SPE and PEARL are dropped from comparison due to OOM errors rather than being adapted/subsampled, weakening the completeness of the PE comparison.

The main-text architecture comparison (Section 5) is limited to five well-known 1-WL-bounded MPNNs; the more informative higher-order (GSN, PPGN) and extended-architecture (GraphGPS, PNA, SGC) results are relegated to the appendix, which somewhat fragments the core empirical narrative and makes it harder to assess how the benchmark performs on more expressive/modern architectures without consulting extensive supplementary material.

The 'statistical significance' criterion for the optimal noise level is based on visually non-overlapping error bars across only 10 runs rather than a formal hypothesis test, which is a relatively soft standard for the central claim that difficulty level determines rankability.

Baseline choices differ somewhat between sections (e.g., only Laplacian PE is used as a baseline in Section 5, while a much richer set of PE methods is introduced in Section 6.2), which could give an inconsistent picture of how strong the 'no-training' or alternative encoding baselines really are throughout the paper.

The claim that graph-topology-based structural benchmarking 'generalizes' to arbitrary downstream tasks is demonstrated only through the positional-encoding and reconstruction pathways (regression and edge reconstruction); no direct evidence is given for other task types (e.g., node/graph classification, generative tasks) where structural understanding might interact differently with features.
